--- title: "Logistic Regression Applications" subtitle: "Build, check, and report a logistic regression analysis from start to finish." description: "A model-building strategy worked through on BRFSS 2020: Table 1, univariable screening, the multivariable model, confounding, effect modification, fit checks, a forest plot, and a publication-ready paragraph." order: 15 unit: "Logistic regression" categories: [Logistic regression] --- ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"} ## Learning objectives By the end of this lecture you will be able to: - follow a seven-step workflow from research question to reported model; - screen candidate predictors and build a multivariable logistic model with gtsummary tables; - assess confounding with the 10% change-in-estimate rule and effect modification with a likelihood ratio test; - check model fit, discrimination, and collinearity before reporting; - write a results paragraph whose wording follows the estimates, and avoid common pitfalls. ::: ## Introduction Over the last three lectures we have built up the machinery of logistic regression: the logit link, odds ratios, multiple predictors, Wald and likelihood ratio tests, interactions, goodness-of-fit, discrimination, and the polytomous and ordinal extensions. Today we put it all together. This is an **applications lecture**. We will work through a complete analytic workflow, from research question to publication-ready table, the way you would for a manuscript or a thesis chapter. ::: {.callout-note} ## Today's roadmap 1. A principled model-building strategy 2. Worked example: building a final model 3. Reporting results for publication 4. Common pitfalls and how to avoid them ::: ## Part 1: A Model-Building Strategy There is no single "correct" way to build a regression model. But there is a sensible workflow that most epidemiologists follow: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Seven-Step Logistic Regression Workflow
Step Phase Tools
1 Define the research question DAG, prior literature, study design
2 Univariable screening Simple glm() per predictor; tbl_uvregression()
3 Build the multivariable model glm() with all candidates; tbl_regression()
4 Assess confounding 10% change-in-estimate rule; compare crude vs adjusted
5 Test interactions * operator; LR test; ggpredict()
6 Check fit and assumptions HL test, calibration, ROC/AUC, Cook's D, VIF
7 Report and interpret tbl_regression(); narrative interpretation
````` ::: ::: ### Two Schools of Thought **Predictive modeling.** Goal: maximize out-of-sample accuracy. Use stepwise selection, LASSO, cross-validation, AUC. The OR is a means to an end. **Etiologic / explanatory modeling.** Goal: estimate the unbiased causal effect of an exposure on an outcome. Use a DAG to choose covariates. Confounders are included; mediators and colliders are excluded. The OR for the exposure is the answer. Most public health research is **etiologic**. Today we adopt that mindset. ## Part 2: Worked Example ### Setup ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(brfssdata) library(broom) library(knitr) library(kableExtra) library(gtsummary) library(car) library(ggeffects) library(ResourceSelection) library(pROC) library(performance) ``` ::: ::: {.column-margin} BRFSS 2020 codebook: [CDC annual data page](https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/annual_2020.html). Package documentation: [brfssdata](https://muntasirmasum.github.io/brfssdata/). ::: ::: {.data-card} [Data for this lecture]{.eyebrow} **BRFSS 2020, loaded with the brfssdata R package.** The first time you run the code below, `read_brfss()` downloads the 2020 survey (about 21 MB) and keeps it on your computer, so later runs read it from there. The code below repeats the recoding and sample from Logistic Regression, Part 1, so this page uses the same 5,000 adults. Install the packages this lecture adds once with `install.packages(c("brfssdata", "janitor", "ResourceSelection", "pROC", "performance"))`. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Read the ten BRFSS 2020 variables this lecture uses (CDC names; # names that start with an underscore need quotes) brfss_full <- read_brfss( 2020, vars = c("MENTHLTH", "PHYSHLTH", "SLEPTIM1", "_AGE80", "SEXVAR", "_BMI5", "EXERANY2", "INCOME2", "SMOKE100", "SMOKDAY2") ) |> janitor::clean_names() ``` ::: The question about current smoking (`SMOKDAY2`) is asked only of people who have smoked at least 100 cigarettes in their life (`SMOKE100`). People who never reached 100 cigarettes are coded as former/never smokers rather than dropped. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} brfss_logistic <- brfss_full |> mutate( # Binary outcome: frequent mental distress (>= 14 days) menthlth_days = case_when( menthlth == 88 ~ 0, menthlth >= 1 & menthlth <= 30 ~ as.numeric(menthlth), TRUE ~ NA_real_ ), fmd = factor( ifelse(menthlth_days >= 14, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes") ), # Predictors physhlth_days = case_when( physhlth == 88 ~ 0, physhlth >= 1 & physhlth <= 30 ~ as.numeric(physhlth), TRUE ~ NA_real_ ), sleep_hrs = case_when( sleptim1 >= 1 & sleptim1 <= 14 ~ as.numeric(sleptim1), TRUE ~ NA_real_ ), age = age80, sex = factor(sexvar, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Male", "Female")), bmi = ifelse(bmi5 > 0, bmi5 / 100, NA_real_), exercise = factor(case_when( exerany2 == 1 ~ "Yes", exerany2 == 2 ~ "No", TRUE ~ NA_character_ ), levels = c("No", "Yes")), income_cat = case_when( income2 %in% 1:8 ~ as.numeric(income2), TRUE ~ NA_real_ ), # SMOKDAY2 is asked only of people who have smoked 100 cigarettes # (SMOKE100 = 1), so people who have not are coded Former/Never smoker = factor(case_when( smoke100 == 2 ~ "Former/Never", smoke100 == 1 & smokday2 %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Current", smoke100 == 1 & smokday2 == 3 ~ "Former/Never", TRUE ~ NA_character_ ), levels = c("Former/Never", "Current")) ) |> filter( !is.na(fmd), !is.na(physhlth_days), !is.na(sleep_hrs), !is.na(age), age >= 18, !is.na(sex), !is.na(bmi), !is.na(exercise), !is.na(income_cat), !is.na(smoker) ) set.seed(1220) brfss_logistic <- brfss_logistic |> dplyr::select(fmd, menthlth_days, physhlth_days, sleep_hrs, age, sex, bmi, exercise, income_cat, smoker) |> slice_sample(n = 5000) ``` ::: ### Research Question > *Among U.S. adults, is any physical activity or exercise in the past 30 days (outside of work) associated with lower odds of frequent mental distress (FMD), after adjusting for demographic, behavioral, and socioeconomic confounders? Does the association differ by sex?* - **Exposure:** `exercise` (Yes / No) - **Outcome:** `fmd` (Yes / No) - **Candidate confounders:** age, sex, BMI, sleep hours, income category, smoking status - **Effect modifier of interest:** sex ### Step 1: Descriptive Table (Table 1) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} brfss_logistic |> tbl_summary( by = fmd, include = c(exercise, age, sex, bmi, sleep_hrs, income_cat, smoker), statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})"), label = list( exercise ~ "Exercise (past 30 days)", age ~ "Age (years)", sex ~ "Sex", bmi ~ "BMI (kg/m²)", sleep_hrs ~ "Sleep (hours)", income_cat ~ "Income category", smoker ~ "Smoking status" ) ) |> add_p(test = all_continuous() ~ "t.test") |> add_overall() |> bold_labels() |> modify_header(label ~ "**Characteristic**") |> modify_caption("Table 1. Sample characteristics by frequent mental distress status.") |> as_kable_extra(escape = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

2 Pearson's Chi-squared test; Welch Two Sample t-test
````` ::: ::: ### Step 2: Univariable Screening ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} brfss_logistic |> tbl_uvregression( method = glm, y = fmd, method.args = list(family = binomial), exponentiate = TRUE, include = c(exercise, age, sex, bmi, sleep_hrs, income_cat, smoker) ) |> bold_labels() |> modify_caption("Table 2. Crude (unadjusted) odds ratios for frequent mental distress.") |> as_kable_extra(escape = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

smoker 5,000

Abbreviations: CI = Confidence Interval, OR = Odds Ratio
````` ::: ::: ### Step 3: Build the Multivariable Model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_full <- glm( fmd ~ exercise + age + sex + bmi + sleep_hrs + income_cat + smoker, data = brfss_logistic, family = binomial ) mod_full |> tbl_regression( exponentiate = TRUE, label = list( exercise ~ "Exercise", age ~ "Age", sex ~ "Sex", bmi ~ "BMI", sleep_hrs ~ "Sleep hours", income_cat ~ "Income category", smoker ~ "Smoker" ) ) |> bold_labels() |> bold_p() |> modify_caption("Table 3. Adjusted odds ratios for frequent mental distress.") |> as_kable_extra(escape = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

Characteristic OR 95% CI p-value
Exercise

Age 0.98 0.98, 0.99 <0.001

Male — —
Female 1.78 1.49, 2.13 <0.001

Income category 0.87 0.83, 0.90 <0.001
Smoker
Former/Never — —
Current 1.64 1.32, 2.02 <0.001
Abbreviations: CI = Confidence Interval, OR = Odds Ratio
````` ::: ::: ### Step 4: Assess Confounding The classic **10% change-in-estimate** rule: a covariate is a confounder of the exposure-outcome relationship if including it changes the exposure OR by more than 10%. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_crude <- glm(fmd ~ exercise, data = brfss_logistic, family = binomial) crude_or <- exp(coef(mod_crude)["exerciseYes"]) adj_or <- exp(coef(mod_full)["exerciseYes"]) pct_change <- 100 * abs(adj_or - crude_or) / crude_or # size of the change tibble( Quantity = c("Crude OR (exercise)", "Adjusted OR (exercise)", "% change in estimate (absolute)"), Value = c(round(crude_or, 3), round(adj_or, 3), paste0(round(pct_change, 1), "%")) ) |> kable(caption = "Change-in-Estimate for Exercise") |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Change-in-Estimate for Exercise
Quantity Value
Crude OR (exercise) 0.7
Adjusted OR (exercise) 0.866
% change in estimate (absolute) 23.7%
````` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Interpretation A change of more than 10% in either direction suggests meaningful confounding by the included covariates; the table reports the size of the change. Here the exercise OR moves from 0.70 (crude) to 0.87 (adjusted), a change of 23.7%, more than 10%, so the covariates confound the association between exercise and FMD. The adjusted OR is closer to 1: part of the crude association reflects differences in age, sex, BMI, sleep, income, and smoking between adults who do and do not exercise. After adjustment the 95% CI for exercise is 0.71 to 1.06, which includes 1. The adjusted OR is the more reliable estimate. ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## Confounder or mediator? The etiologic approach in Part 1 leaves mediators out of the model, yet the model above adjusts for sleep hours and BMI. Exercise can improve sleep and lower BMI, so both may lie on the path from exercise to mental distress. Adjusting for a mediator removes part of the effect we want to estimate, so part of the change from the crude OR may not be confounding. Leaving sleep and BMI out (adjusting for age, sex, income, and smoking only) gives an exercise OR of 0.80 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.98). A DAG drawn before the analysis is how to decide which model answers the research question. ::: ### Step 5: Test for Effect Modification by Sex ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_int <- glm( fmd ~ exercise * sex + age + bmi + sleep_hrs + income_cat + smoker, data = brfss_logistic, family = binomial ) lr_int <- anova(mod_full, mod_int, test = "LRT") lr_int |> kable(digits = 3, caption = "LR Test: Exercise × Sex Interaction") |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
LR Test: Exercise × Sex Interaction
Resid. Df Resid. Dev Df Deviance Pr(>Chi)
4992 3565.882 NA NA NA
4991 3565.261 1 0.621 0.431
````` ::: ::: The LR statistic is 0.62 on 1 df (p = 0.431), so there is no evidence that the association between exercise and FMD differs by sex. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggpredict(mod_int, terms = c("exercise", "sex")) |> plot() + labs(title = "Predicted Probability of FMD by Exercise and Sex", x = "Exercise", y = "Predicted Probability", color = "Sex") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](logistic-applications_files/figure-html/interaction-plot-1.png){fig-alt='Dot-and-interval plot of the predicted probability of FMD by exercise (No, Yes) and sex. Women are higher at both levels, about 15% without exercise and 13% with it; men are about 8% at both levels. The 95% intervals for adults who do not exercise are wide.' width=768} ::: ::: ### Stratum-Specific Estimates If the interaction is meaningful, report ORs **within each level of sex**: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_male <- glm( fmd ~ exercise + age + bmi + sleep_hrs + income_cat + smoker, data = filter(brfss_logistic, sex == "Male"), family = binomial ) mod_female <- glm( fmd ~ exercise + age + bmi + sleep_hrs + income_cat + smoker, data = filter(brfss_logistic, sex == "Female"), family = binomial ) strata <- bind_rows( tidy(mod_male, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == "exerciseYes") |> mutate(stratum = "Male"), tidy(mod_female, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term == "exerciseYes") |> mutate(stratum = "Female") ) # ORs implied by the interaction model (the model the LR test in Step 5 uses) b <- coef(mod_int) or_int <- c(Male = exp(b[["exerciseYes"]]), Female = exp(b[["exerciseYes"]] + b[["exerciseYes:sexFemale"]])) strata |> dplyr::select(stratum, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |> mutate(across(c(estimate, conf.low, conf.high), \(x) round(x, 3)), p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3)) |> kable(col.names = c("Sex", "OR (Exercise)", "Lower", "Upper", "p"), caption = "Stratum-Specific ORs for Exercise") |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Stratum-Specific ORs for Exercise
Sex OR (Exercise) Lower Upper p
Male 1.020 0.729 1.446 0.912
Female 0.784 0.609 1.012 0.060
````` ::: ::: Here the exercise OR is 1.02 among men and 0.78 among women. These come from separate models for men and women, which let every covariate's effect differ by sex. The interaction model tested in Step 5 lets only the exercise effect differ; its ORs are 0.96 for men and 0.82 for women. The point estimates differ, but the interaction test found no evidence that the difference is larger than chance, so the single adjusted OR from Step 3 is the main result; the stratum-specific ORs are shown for transparency. ### Step 6: Check Fit and Assumptions ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_stats <- list( `McFadden R²` = round(performance::r2_mcfadden(mod_full)$R2, 3), `HL p-value` = round(hoslem.test( x = as.numeric(brfss_logistic$fmd) - 1, y = fitted(mod_full), g = 10)$p.value, 3), `AUC` = round(as.numeric(auc(roc( brfss_logistic$fmd, fitted(mod_full), levels = c("No", "Yes"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))), 3), `Max VIF` = round(max(car::vif(mod_full)), 2) ) tibble(Measure = names(fit_stats), Value = unlist(fit_stats)) |> kable(caption = "Fit and Diagnostic Summary") |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = "striped", full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Fit and Diagnostic Summary
Measure Value
McFadden R² 0.078
HL p-value 0.864
AUC 0.700
Max VIF 1.110
````` ::: ::: McFadden's R² is 0.078. The Hosmer-Lemeshow test finds no evidence of lack of fit (p = 0.864). The AUC of 0.700 is at the boundary between poor and acceptable discrimination on the scale from Logistic Regression, Part 2. The largest VIF is 1.11, so collinearity is not a concern. ### Step 7: Forest Plot of Final Model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} term_names <- c(exerciseYes = "Exercise", age = "Age", sexFemale = "Female sex", bmi = "BMI", sleep_hrs = "Sleep hours", income_cat = "Income category", smokerCurrent = "Current smoker") tidy(mod_full, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)") |> ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = fct_reorder(term_names[term], estimate))) + geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") + geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) + scale_x_log10() + labs(title = "Adjusted Odds Ratios for Frequent Mental Distress", x = "Adjusted OR (log scale)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](logistic-applications_files/figure-html/forest-1.png){fig-alt='Forest plot of adjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals on a log-scale x-axis, with a dashed grey reference line at 1. From largest to smallest: female sex about 1.8, current smoking about 1.6, BMI just above 1, age just below 1, income and exercise about 0.87, and sleep hours about 0.79. Current smoking and exercise have the widest intervals; exercise\'s, about 0.71 to 1.06, is the only one that crosses 1.' width=768} ::: ::: ## Part 3: Reporting Results ### A Publication-Ready Paragraph The paragraph below is written from the estimates above; every number and every direction word comes from the model output. > *In adjusted models, current smokers had 1.64 times the odds of frequent mental distress compared with former or never smokers (aOR = 1.64; 95% CI: 1.32, 2.02). Each additional hour of sleep was associated with 21% lower odds of FMD (aOR = 0.79; 95% CI: 0.74, 0.84). Exercise was associated with lower odds of FMD before adjustment (crude OR = 0.70), but after adjustment for demographic, behavioral, and socioeconomic covariates the association was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (aOR = 0.87; 95% CI: 0.71, 1.06). The likelihood ratio test for an exercise × sex interaction was not statistically significant (p = 0.431; exercise ORs from the interaction model 0.96 for men and 0.82 for women), so the data provide no evidence that the association with exercise differs by sex.* ### What Every Logistic Regression Paper Should Report 1. **Sample size and outcome prevalence** 2. **Table 1** stratified by outcome 3. **Crude and adjusted ORs** with 95% CIs (not just p-values) 4. **Which covariates were included and why** (DAG, prior literature, change-in-estimate) 5. **Tests of effect modification** that were planned 6. **Goodness-of-fit and discrimination** metrics (HL or calibration plot, AUC) 7. **Software and packages** with versions ## Part 4: Common Pitfalls ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Common Pitfalls in Logistic Regression
Pitfall Fix
Reporting p-values without ORs and CIs Always show point estimates with 95% CIs
Stepwise selection on small samples Use a DAG; pre-specify covariates
Adjusting for mediators Draw a DAG; do not adjust on the causal pathway
Adjusting for colliders Avoid conditioning on common effects of exposure and outcome
Ignoring the events-per-variable rule (EPV < 10) Aim for ≥ 10 events per predictor; use penalized methods if not
Interpreting OR as relative risk when outcome is common Use log-binomial or modified Poisson when prevalence > ~10%
Forgetting to check linearity in the logit Restricted cubic splines or LOWESS-of-logit plots
Reporting only the p-value of an interaction Always show stratum-specific estimates
````` ::: ::: ## Summary | Step | Key Action | |------|-----------| | **1. Question** | Anchor your model in a clear research question and DAG | | **2. Screen** | Univariable models inform but do not select | | **3. Build** | Include confounders identified a priori | | **4. Confound** | Compare crude vs adjusted; 10% rule of thumb | | **5. Modify** | Plan interactions; report stratum-specific estimates | | **6. Check** | Fit, calibration, discrimination, diagnostics | | **7. Report** | ORs + CIs, narrative interpretation, full transparency | ### Next Lecture - Poisson regression for count outcomes - Survival analysis: an introduction ## References - Kleinbaum, D. G., Kupper, L. L., Nizam, A., & Rosenberg, E. S. (2013). *Applied Regression Analysis and Other Multivariable Methods* (5th ed.), Chapters 22-23. - Hosmer, D. W., Lemeshow, S., & Sturdivant, R. X. (2013). *Applied Logistic Regression* (3rd ed.). Wiley. - Vittinghoff, E., et al. (2012). *Regression Methods in Biostatistics* (2nd ed.). Springer. - Greenland, S. (1989). Modeling and variable selection in epidemiologic analysis. *American Journal of Public Health*, 79(3), 340-349. *No lab activity for this lecture: you have practiced this workflow in the previous three labs.* ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Session info ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24) Platform: aarch64-apple-darwin23 Running under: macOS Golden Gate 27.2.1 Matrix products: default BLAS: ~/.uvr/r-versions/4.6.1/lib/libRblas.0.dylib LAPACK: ~/.uvr/r-versions/4.6.1/lib/libRlapack.dylib;
